# Process and execution

Working definition for this standard: a **process** is an organized set of activities through which participants use inputs to produce an intended result.

The fuller description explains how work proceeds: its responsibilities, decisions, states, transitions and conditions. An intended result does not mean that every execution achieves it. This page is a developing proposal; its fields and examples are not yet an accepted mandatory schema.

## What we are describing

A **process description** describes how a process operates or is intended to operate. State whether it describes existing practice, intended behavior, or an explicitly distinguished comparison of the two. It can describe responsibilities, activities, decisions, states, transitions, conditions, handoffs and completion criteria; the required information remains under review. The [BPMN source account](../../../../source-locators.md#source-b3674e2872c64d49) supports both descriptive uses without selecting BPMN as our schema. An **execution** is a particular occurrence of that work, involving actual participants, inputs, conditions and results. A **record** represents some part of what happened and can be incomplete or inaccurate. An **assessment** judges a result against a requirement or other stated criterion using available evidence.

For example, a description can specify how to transfer data; an execution is one requested transfer; its log is a record; a judgment about whether the required data arrived correctly and on time is an assessment. A process can be used once, repeatedly or continuously; recurrence is not required by this definition.

## Candidate process description

These eight groups organize the information we have already discussed. Requiredness and exact field names remain open. Information can be linked from its owning definition rather than copied. Missing information should be visible; absence does not mean not applicable.

| Part | Information to describe |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose, scope and requirements | Why the process exists; where its responsibility begins and ends; intended results; related needs and requirements; why it is expected to contribute. |
| Ownership and responsibility | Who maintains the process and answers for its operation; who performs activities; who may decide exceptions, approve changes and accept results; the limits of each authority. |
| Trigger and prerequisites | What starts or continues the work; required inputs and their readiness; authorization; relevant resources, dependencies, conditions and constraints. |
| Activities and decisions | What happens, including decision criteria, alternatives, sequence, repetition and concurrency where relevant. |
| States and transitions | The subject whose state is described; what each state means; what permits progression; what happens when work cannot progress. |
| Handoffs and exceptions | Producer and recipient; what passes between them; when it is usable; acceptance of the handoff; responsibility for missing input, failure and escalation. |
| Outputs and completion | Intended outputs or changes; completion, stopping and continuation criteria; the distinction between finishing the work, satisfying requirements and accepting results. |
| Execution history and assessment | How to connect a particular execution to the applicable description/revision, actual actors, inputs, conditions, events, outputs and decisions, and to records and assessments about them. |

The last group describes what needs to be retrievable about executions. It does not put every execution log inside the reusable process description or require a universal event log.

## Ownership and continuing responsibility

“Owner” needs an explicit remit. Maintaining the process description, answering for operation, performing one execution, authorizing an exception and accepting a result can be different responsibilities. One person may hold several; the model should still make the responsibilities understandable.

The description states the role and authority arrangement and its basis; describing an assignment does not itself grant authority. A particular execution identifies the actual actors filling those roles. Completing one execution does not necessarily end the continuing responsibility: finishing this month's payment process does not end responsibility for future pay periods. Shared ownership, delegation and changes of owner still need rules; naming an owner alone does not settle them.

The general meaning of these responsibilities belongs in [actors and roles](actors-and-roles.md). Their use at a handoff belongs in [execution and responsibility](../../execution/behavior-and-responsibility.md).

## States, events and transitions

State always has a subject and an applicable time or interval. Keep these uses distinguishable:

| Subject | Illustrative states or results |
| --- | --- |
| Process description | Draft or approved: the standing of the description. |
| Particular execution | Waiting, transferring, checking, completed, blocked or failed: the condition of that execution. |
| Requirement assessment | Met, unmet or unknown for the criterion; extent of achievement is reported separately under the accepted [assessment contract](../../assessment/requirement-and-need-fulfillment.md). |

These are examples, not a common state vocabulary. A state such as “waiting” also needs a meaning: waiting for what, who can resolve it, and what ends the wait. “Completed” must state what was completed. An assessment may be unknown even when the execution is recorded as completed.

A candidate transition description identifies the starting and resulting states, the event or decision that can cause the change, the conditions that permit it, and the role or mechanism authorized to act where an action or decision is required. An external event, such as a network failure, can change state without authorization; identify who is responsible for responding. When useful, it also identifies required actions, their results, and what happens if progression fails. An intended process description can state allowed behavior; a description of existing practice describes how work operates. Execution records represent particular observed behavior, including departures from the applicable intended description. A description of existing practice does not itself authorize that practice. A record of a transition does not by itself prove the transition was permitted or successful.

Relevant events can include receipt of an input, an approval, a failure or a handoff. Events and states are related, but not interchangeable. Their general definitions and evidence limits remain in [occurrences and state](occurrences-and-state.md).

## How a process fits into a system

A process explains how work proceeds within or across an arrangement. It may be part of a larger process, use resources, depend on another process's output, and contribute to a system's intended results. These relations mean different things: depending on something does not automatically make it a part; a claimed contribution needs a reason.

A structure is an arrangement of elements and relationships; its description represents that arrangement. It does not, by itself, specify the progression of work. A process participating in a system is not automatically a subtype of system. See [system](system.md), [structure](structure.md), [composition](../../mereology/composition-and-boundaries.md) and the candidate [relationship vocabulary](../relationships.md). The exact boundaries with workflow, procedure and system behavior remain open.

## Illustrative data-transfer process

This hypothetical example tests the description; it is not a claim about an implemented transfer system or observed performance.

| Part | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and requirements | Make a requested dataset available at an authorized destination, unchanged, by the deadline specified in the request. |
| Ownership | An operating role maintains the process and answers for unresolved transfers; an operator or service performs each transfer; a named authority handles exceptions; a recipient role accepts delivery. These may be held by the same person. |
| Trigger and prerequisites | An authorized request identifies the dataset, destination and deadline. The source is readable, the destination is writable, and necessary resources are available. A missing prerequisite prevents progression and is assigned for resolution. |
| Activities | Check the request, transfer the data, check integrity, and notify the recipient. Missing input or failure leads to an explicit decision to resolve, retry, escalate or stop. |
| States and transitions | Waiting → transferring when prerequisites hold; transferring → checking when copying ends; checking → completed when integrity is confirmed and notification is issued. A detected integrity failure cannot take that final transition. Blocking, failure, cancellation and retry paths need their own conditions and authority. |
| Handoffs | The recipient receives a usable destination reference and the relevant integrity result. Receipt of a notification is distinct from accepting delivery. |
| Completion and fulfillment | Here, completed means the specified work and checks finished. Data can arrive intact after the required deadline: this execution can be completed while its timing requirement is unmet. A local completion label does not override the requirement. |
| History and assessment | Retain the applicable process and requirement revisions, actual request and participants, relevant times and conditions, transfer/check records, exceptions and acceptance decisions. Evaluate integrity and timing separately; missing timing evidence leaves timing fulfillment unknown. |

A transfer tool by itself does not describe this process: it leaves responsibility, request handling, conditions and handoffs unexplained. Likewise, evidence that one transfer succeeded does not establish reliability across future transfers. Coverage, reliability, quality, conditions, evidence confidence and acceptance remain separate in [fulfillment assessment](../../assessment/requirement-and-need-fulfillment.md).
